# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
#
# Rediscovers the similarity audit's targets every month (R-AUDIT-2;
# docs/AUDIT.md, "Rediscovery"). tools/audit-discover.py reads repository
# metadata only, never a target's code. When a target is new, gone or has a
# new head commit, this opens a pull request that changes
# audit/targets.json and lists those repositories by name. GitHub does not
# run CI for a pull request a workflow opens: the owner closes and reopens
# it to start `ci`, then merges it as usual.
name: audit-discover

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "17 5 1 * *"
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: audit-discover
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  discover:
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    timeout-minutes: 60
    permissions:
      contents: write
      pull-requests: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1

      - uses: actions/setup-python@6d4fd22b20465ccc0f7354476588e8df7c9ca0e0 # v7.1.0
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      - name: Rediscover the targets (metadata only)
        id: discover
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: |
          set +e
          python tools/audit-discover.py --write > "$RUNNER_TEMP/discover.txt"
          status=$?
          cat "$RUNNER_TEMP/discover.txt"
          echo "status=$status" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - name: Open a pull request with the changes
        if: steps.discover.outputs.status == '1'
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: |
          set -eu
          branch="audit/rediscover-$(date -u +%Y-%m-%d)-$GITHUB_RUN_ID"
          git checkout -q -b "$branch"
          git add audit/targets.json
          {
            echo "audit: rediscovered targets, $(date -u +%Y-%m-%d)"
            echo
            echo "What:    audit/targets.json updated by the monthly rediscovery."
            echo "Why:     R-AUDIT-2: every FM-1 repository found from metadata is pinned."
            echo "How:     tools/audit-discover.py --write, metadata only (docs/AUDIT.md)."
            echo "Result:  see the pull request: new, gone and moved repositories by name."
            echo "Sources: none"
            echo "Exposure: none (a workflow; repository metadata only)"
          } > "$RUNNER_TEMP/msg.txt"
          git -c user.name="small-beeps audit-discover" -c user.email="audit-discover@users.noreply.github.com" \
            commit -q -F "$RUNNER_TEMP/msg.txt"
          git push -q origin "$branch"
          {
            echo "**What:** the monthly rediscovery of the similarity audit's targets (docs/AUDIT.md), from repository metadata only."
            echo
            echo '```'
            cat "$RUNNER_TEMP/discover.txt"
            echo '```'
            echo
            echo "**Run:** $GITHUB_SERVER_URL/$GITHUB_REPOSITORY/actions/runs/$GITHUB_RUN_ID"
            echo
            echo "GitHub does not start CI for a pull request a workflow opens: close and reopen this one to run \`ci\`."
          } > "$RUNNER_TEMP/body.md"
          gh pr create --base main --head "$branch" \
            --title "audit: rediscovered targets, $(date -u +%Y-%m-%d)" --body-file "$RUNNER_TEMP/body.md"

python3 - <<'EOF'
p='docs/HARNESS.md'; s=open(p).read()
start=s.index("## Time\n"); end=s.index("## The command line")
new='''## Time

- Emulated time starts at 0 when the image starts. One instruction of core 0
  takes one cycle; there are 240 000 cycles in an emulated millisecond.
- Everything happens at exact emulated times, and the outputs are
  deterministic (below), but **while core 0 waits, fwtest moves time ahead**,
  so that waiting costs (almost) no instructions and instruction counts
  measure work. The rules for that, and what they do to captures, are
  exact; they follow.

### When fwtest treats core 0 as waiting

Two things, and nothing else, count as waiting:

1. **The wait-for-interrupt instruction**, executed by core 0 while no
   interrupt is pending. Time jumps to one cycle before the next scheduled
   event (below). With nothing scheduled, time doesn't jump.
2. **Polling the free-running timer**: reading its count (HW-13 in
   `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, the 24 MHz time base), outside an interrupt handler
   of core 0, for the third time or more in a row with each read coming
   within 64 cycles (64 instructions of core 0) of the one before. On each
   such read, time jumps ahead by up to 20 µs, and never past one cycle
   before the next scheduled event. The read then returns the count for
   the new time.
   - **Only the spacing of the reads matters.** What the loop does between
     them doesn't: stores to RAM, arithmetic, reads of other registers, a
     call. A loop that reads the count every few instructions *and* writes
     a heartbeat to RAM on every pass is waiting, by this rule.
   - A read more than 64 cycles after the previous one starts the count
     again, so a loop whose reads are at least 64 instructions apart is
     never treated as waiting.
   - Reads made while core 0 is in an interrupt handler neither count nor
     jump.
   - Reads by core 1 count in the same sequence as core 0's: the rule
     looks at reads of the count, not at which core made them.
   - Other timers' counters, their pending flags, and RAM flags are not
     part of this rule. Polling them never moves time ahead.

**Scheduled events** are what the emulated chip and the script have coming
next:
- the end of a timer period;
- an audio half-buffer finishing;
- a transfer completing;
- a MIDI byte arriving;
- an encoder contact changing;
- a script event.

They count whether or not their interrupt is enabled. **Captures, the end
of the run and the watchdog are not scheduled events:** a jump never stops
for them.

### What that does to captures

- fwtest looks at the board between runs of core 0 instructions. Each run
  is at most 1024 instructions, and no longer than the instructions that
  would reach the next capture (or the end of the run) at one cycle each.
  Captures, the watchdog, halts and the end of the run are checked only
  between runs. A capture is taken at the first such stop at or after its
  time.
- **While core 0 is busy (not waiting), captures are exact:** taken at the
  first instruction boundary at or after the time asked.
- **While core 0 waits, a capture can come late**, because every jump
  inside a run moves time without using up the run's instructions:
  - Polling the timer: each read can add up to 20 µs. A loop that reads the
    count every *k* instructions can move up to about 1024 / *k* × 20 µs in
    one run, for example 2 ms when *k* is 10. A capture asked for at *t*
    can be taken that much after *t*.
  - Wait-for-interrupt: each wait jumps to the next scheduled event. A run
    that wakes on every event can cross many of them, for example several
    milliseconds of 100 µs interrupts.
- What is late is the moment the capture is taken, not its label. RAM and
  screen captures show the state at the moment fwtest took them, but are
  named for the time asked (`ram-…-10ms.bin`). `leds.csv`'s `ms` column is
  the time asked, while each duty value covers the real time since the
  previous sample. The end of the run, and so every `end` capture, can come
  late in the same way. `result.json`'s `emulated_ms` says when the run
  really ended.
- The watchdog compares its word between runs, so a hang is noticed up to
  one run late.
- None of this varies between runs: the same image, script and options give
  the same late times, byte for byte, everywhere.

### Getting exact timing

- **Don't wait around the times you capture.** Keep core 0 busy then, for
  example by spacing reads of the timer's count at least 64 instructions
  apart, or by waiting on something else: another timer's pending flag, or
  a RAM flag that an interrupt handler sets. Captures are then exact.
- **Or let the image record the time itself.** Store the timer's count (or
  your own tick count) next to what you capture, and check the capture
  against that stored time instead of the time asked. The M0d firmware's
  beacon does this (docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md).
- **For the end of a run**, read `emulated_ms` in `result.json`.
- Instruction counts (`instructions` in `result.json`, `ipb.csv`) do not
  include the time jumped over: a waiting image's counts stay small and
  stable.

'''
s=s[:start]+new+s[end:]
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF

docs: HARNESS.md says exactly when fwtest treats core 0 as waiting

What:    Rewrites docs/HARNESS.md's "Time" section. It says exactly which
         two things count as waiting (the wait-for-interrupt instruction,
         and polling the free-running timer's count, judged by the spacing
         of the reads alone), how far each jump goes, that captures, the
         end of the run and the watchdog are not events a jump stops for,
         how late a capture can come and what its file name and leds.csv
         then mean, and how a test gets exact timing.
Why:     M0e (spec part), "timer polling": the clean side saw a heartbeat
         loop that stores to RAM on every pass counted as waiting, with
         captures up to 1.6 ms late. The old text said a waiting loop "does
         nothing but read" the timer, which was wrong; the behaviour itself
         is as designed (waiting costs no instructions, so instruction
         counts measure work) and deterministic. R-HARN-3, R-HARN-6.
How:     Read from the harness and the emulator it carries, and written as
         black-box behaviour: a 64-cycle spacing, a 20 us cap per read, a
         jump to just before the next scheduled event, runs of up to 1024
         instructions. No harness change, so no new image: making captures
         exact would change capture times, and with them golden files on
         both sides. That is left as an option for the owner.
Result:  check-emulator-terms.py: PASS (no new term in the door).

- Read from the harness and the emulator it carries, and written as black-box behaviour only.
- No harness change, so no new image. Exact captures while waiting would need fwtest to stop time at each capture. That changes when captures are taken, and with them golden files on both sides (the firmware's boot suite, the spec experiments). It is left as an option for the owner.

new='''def score(pairs, cfg, where):
    """Splits JPlag's pairs by kind and applies the gate. Pairs are
    (a, b, longest, max, avg) with a and b named o.. (ours), c.. (control)
    or p.. (a target file); where maps a target file to its (repo, path)s.

    The baseline is the control's longest match with any target it is not
    related to; a target the control itself matches above the ceiling is
    control-related, and is judged against the control's own score there.
    A pair of ours fails above its target's score plus the margin (for a
    file several targets hold, the strictest of theirs)."""
    ours, ctl, ours_ctl = [], [], []
    for a, b, l, m, v in pairs:
        k = {a[0], b[0]}
        if k == {"o", "p"}:
            o, p = (a, b) if a[0] == "o" else (b, a)
            ours.append((o, p, l, m, v))
        elif k == {"c", "p"}:
            c, p = (a, b) if a[0] == "c" else (b, a)
            ctl.append((c, p, l, m, v))
        elif k == {"o", "c"}:
            o, c = (a, b) if a[0] == "o" else (b, a)
            ours_ctl.append((o, c, l, m, v))
    best = lambda xs: sorted(xs, key=lambda x: (-x[2], -x[3], x[0], x[1]))
    per_target = {}
    for c, p, l, m, v in ctl:
        for repo, _ in where.get(p, []):
            per_target[repo] = max(per_target.get(repo, 0), l)
    related = sorted(r for r, l in per_target.items() if l > cfg["control_ceiling_tokens"])
    baseline = max([l for r, l in per_target.items() if r not in related], default=0)

    def threshold(p):
        return min([(per_target[r] if r in related else baseline) + cfg["margin_tokens"]
                    for r, _ in where.get(p, [])] or [baseline + cfg["margin_tokens"]])

    flagged = [x for x in best(ours) if x[2] > threshold(x[1])]
    return {"ours": best(ours), "control": best(ctl), "ours_control": best(ours_ctl),
            "control_max": baseline, "threshold": baseline + cfg["margin_tokens"], "flagged": flagged,
            "related": related, "control_per_target": per_target}

- **Similarity audit** (spec side): an isolated CI job fetches the GPL
  firmwares at pinned commits, compares our firmware against them with JPlag
  (SDK as base code, `vendor/` excluded, an unrelated permissive embedded C
  project scored as a control), and publishes scores and file names only.
- **Performance tracking** (firmware side): per-commit size and RAM, later
  emulated instructions per audio block. A 3% regression gate on
  instructions per audio block; per-milestone budgets for size and RAM,
  raised only by a pull request that says why.
- Requirements: R-AUDIT-1, R-PERF-1 to R-PERF-5.
- Status 2026-10-22, performance part (session M0e, firmware side, on the

    high-water mark, and emulated core-0 instructions per period. Until
    M4 the period is the heartbeat: a one-second perf run of its own in
    fwtest, its instructions divided by the beats. The stack's mark is

    milestone, and a rise of at most 3% in instructions per period

    static RAM 280 and stack high-water 516 bytes (each FAIL).

    252, static RAM 24, stack high-water 0, 356.887 instructions per
    heartbeat period). This pull request's merge adds the second.
  - The similarity audit is the spec side's part of M0e. M1 is next on

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
